posts.title: When a student says, “I can’t draw.”
posts.imageAlt: Checklist illustration from Torch and Trowel
posts.excerpt: Treat “I can’t draw” as a signal that the task feels too big. Shrink the next move until the student can begin again.
posts.when: Use this when a student freezes, wants you to judge the whole drawing, or starts comparing their page to someone else’s.
tryThis: Cover part of the page with your hand or another sheet of paper.
Choose one small area: one line, one box, one edge, or one shape.
Ask the student to make only that part a little clearer.
posts.why: A stuck student usually needs a smaller decision, not a bigger explanation. Narrowing the task lowers pressure and returns attention to observation.
posts.script: “Let’s not decide if the whole drawing is good. Point to one line you can make more intentional.”

posts.title: When the worksheet gets rushed.
posts.excerpt: Finishing every box quickly is not the same as practicing. Use one repeated box to slow the lesson down without making it feel like punishment.
posts.when: Use this when a student fills the page fast, scribbles through the prompts, or tries to be done before they have looked carefully.
tryThis: Pick one box that already exists on the worksheet.
Have the student repeat only that box slowly beside it or on the back of the page.
Compare the fast version and the slow version without scolding.
posts.why: A single repeated box preserves momentum while making attention visible. The student can see the difference between speed and control.
posts.script: “You finished the page. Now let’s choose one box and make a slower version so your hand can catch up with your eyes.”

posts.title: How to help without hovering.
posts.imageAlt: Technique tips illustration from Torch and Trowel
posts.excerpt: The support guide should help you notice what to say next, not turn you into a constant commentator.
posts.when: Use this when you find yourself correcting every mark, explaining too much, or sitting beside the student longer than the lesson needs.
tryThis: Check the support guide before the student begins.
Choose one thing you will watch for during the lesson.
Wait until the student asks or reaches a natural pause before offering help.
posts.why: Students need room to make decisions. A parent’s job is to redirect attention, not narrate every mark on the page.
posts.script: “I’m going to let you work for a few minutes. If you get stuck, I’ll help you look at the guide.”

posts.title: Why the early lessons do not need rulers.
posts.excerpt: A ruler can make a line straight, but it cannot teach the student to control pressure, direction, rhythm, or confidence.
posts.when: Use this when a student wants a tool to make the page look cleaner before they have practiced hand control.
tryThis: Ask for a slow hand-drawn line instead of a perfect line.
Have the student draw the same kind of line three times.
Look for steadier pressure, not mechanical straightness.
posts.why: Early drawing practice is about hand, eye, and attention working together. Slightly imperfect lines are useful evidence.
posts.script: “The goal is not a machine-straight line. The goal is a line your hand meant to make.”

posts.title: When circles on cups look wrong.
posts.excerpt: Openings on cups, bowls, and jars often look odd because students draw the symbol of a circle instead of the shape they actually see.
posts.when: Use this when a student’s cup opening turns into a flat football, a pointed eye shape, or a circle that ignores the angle of the object.
tryThis: Have the student trace the air above the opening with a finger.
Ask which side of the ellipse feels wider, flatter, or more open.
Draw the ellipse lightly two or three times before darkening one version.
posts.why: Ellipses improve when students observe the angle and width of the opening instead of relying on a memorized circle shape.
posts.script: “Do not draw the idea of a circle. Look at the opening and draw the shape it is making from where you sit.”

posts.title: Shapes before forms.
posts.excerpt: Students draw objects better when they first learn to find simple flat shapes, then build those shapes into forms.
posts.when: Use this when a student wants to draw a complicated object all at once and gets lost in details.
tryThis: Ask the student to find the largest simple shape first.
Ignore texture and small details for one pass.
Add form only after the basic shape relationship is clear.
posts.why: Simple shapes reduce visual overwhelm. Once the big shapes are placed, form and detail have somewhere to belong.
posts.script: “Before we draw the object, let’s find the simple shape hiding inside it.”
